The correct answer is E: vasculogenesis.  Vascular development occurs in two stages: vasculogenesis and angiogenesis. Vasculogenesis is the formation of new blood vessels from endothelial cells in the embryo, a process inhibited by lithium. This results in a lack of extraembryonic Vasculature and can result in spina bifida (hence 50% of neural tube defects are caused by lithium, and 40% are spina bifida).  Arborisation is the subsequent phase of vascular development, in which the primary haema-angioblasts develop into a more complex network of vessels. Haematopoiesis is the formation of blood cells in the bone marrow (the yolk sac is the first site of haematopoiesis, followed by the bone marrow in later gestation). Somatogenesis is the development of the individual fertilised cells into an organism, including the development of the digestive, respiratory, circulatory, and urogenital systems.

Together with the macrophages, dendritic cells and Langerhans cells, these four cell types are known as the 'immunity guys' as they all function as sentinels - meaning they monitor for intrusion. When an intracellular pathogen is detected, these cells all have the ability to phagocytose it and/or present the pathogen's antigen(s) on MHC I and II molecules respectively to T cells.  Natural killer cells (NK cells) are another type of lymphocyte, but they are part of the adaptive immune system, whereas the sentinel cells are part of the innate immune system. NK cells monitor for viral cytopathic effects and can kill target cells by inducing granzymes and perforins, or by engaging Fas receptor mediated cell death.

Carnitine acyltransferase I (CAT I) is the correct answer!  CAT I is found on the outer mitochondrial membrane and is the enzyme that catalyses the reaction between Acyl-CoA and carnitine. This forms acylcarnitine, which is then transferred across the mitochondrial membrane by an acylcarnitine-translocase.  On the inner mitochondrial membrane, CAT II catalyses the reaction between acylcarnitine and CoA, regenerating acyl-CoA and carnitine.  The five key enzymes of beta-oxidation are:1. Acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (catalyse the oxidation of acyl-CoA to- enoyl-CoA by the removal of 2 H atoms)2. Enoyl-CoA hydratase (catalyse the addition of water across the double bond to form L-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA)3. L-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase (catalyse the oxidation of L-3-hydroxyacyl-CoA to R-3-ketoacyl-CoA)4. Acyl-CoA acetylase (catalyse the splitting of R-2-ketoacyl-CoA into acetyl-CoA and a shorter fatty acyl-CoA)5. Carnitine acyltransferase I (catalyse the formation of acylcarnitine from acyl-CoA and carnitine)

The correct answer is the quadruple test. This is because this test has the lowest accuracy but the lowest invasive risk. It detects levels of four proteins (AFP,beta-hCG,uE3 and INH-A) in the mothers urine and is therefore the most appropriate in this situation due to Betjys high BMI.  In women with a BMI >30kg/m2, the triple test should be replaced with the:Spontaneous Abort Loss (SAL) test:measures levels of PAPP-A, beta-hCG and PlGF in the mothers blood. The combined test:measures nuchal translucency, beta-hCG and PAPP-A in the mothers blood. The invasive tests either removed or may be offered are:Amniocentesis:Performed at 13-20 weeks, involves taking a sample of foetal cells from the amniotic sac.May be performed 19-22 weeks in high risk cases.Chorionic Villus Sampling (CVS):Performed at 11-13 weeks, involves taking a sample of extraembryonic trophoblast cells from the placenta. +/- 18 weeks.
